To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RBF sites in India are at high risk from untreated river water and groundwater, and that risk-based assessments and management are a useful framework for RBF site management.

(i) the risks from untreated Ganga River water and groundwater are high; (ii) the risks of recovered water are lower but still high; (iii) the risks from recovered water are below the national diarrheal incidence and meet the health risk target; and (iv) a water safety plan has been developed to reduce risks further.
RBF is a viable option to treat raw water from the Ganges River, and a risk-based approach can be applied to assess the risks to human health and environment from RBF sites in India and elsewhere.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of a comprehensive risk-based approach to RBF sites in India and the development of a water safety plan.
the application of a systematic and structured framework for the assessment and management of risks associated with RBF sites, which is consistent with the Australian Guidelines for MAR.
the application of risk-based assessment to RBF schemes and the development of water safety plans to reduce residual risks to the community.

the risks from the RBF sites are low, with the exception of pathogens.
RBF is safe and effective at the RBF sites assessed in this study, and that RBF can be used for safe and reliable drinking water supply in India.
the RBF scheme at the study site is safe to use for drinking water supply and meets the national health targets for diarrhoea and other water-borne diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risks from untreated Ganga River water to public health are significant and can be managed through a staged risk-based assessment and a water safety plan.
the risks from RBF sites in India are low but can be managed through appropriate risk management strategies.
RBF is a feasible option for water recovery in the Indian context, provided that the water recovered from RBF sites is disinfected to reduce pathogenic risks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a risk-based assessment approach can be applied to an RBF site in India to identify the main sources of risk and to develop risk management options for a water safety plan.
a comprehensive assessment of RBF sites in India can be undertaken using Australian guidelines.
a risk-based approach can be used to assess the safety of water recovered from RBF systems and to develop a water safety plan for a RBF site.
